Motivated by this idea, and by the empirically observed asymmetry between parent-anchored and child-anchored witness-overlap distributions, we propose Witness Overlap, a prompt-free, training-free white-box test for directional provenance. On 176 LLM checkpoints from 16 families, our one-witness test orients 95.3\% of parent-child decisions using Frobenius cosine. We further evaluate root identification, sibling discrimination, generaliza

f4e25a990d01591ed27485b6.title_original: From Migration to Calibration: Aligning Agents with Deployment Requirements
f4e25a990d01591ed27485b6.excerpt: arXiv:2609.35149v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deploying, migrating, or scaling an agent changes its model, support system, application, and users. Calibration should align the agent with destination requirements without requiring source imitation or universal superiority. We propose three standard families: basic capability and operational reachability; technical and professional precision, including terminology, units, reporting periods, program fidelity, and report dependencies; and user context covering roles, use cases, authorized values, permissions, and budgets. A versioned mapping distinguishes requirements to preserve, transform, add, or retire. Four instruments---benchmarks, positive/negative examples, skills, and role-conditioned cost/utility---supply tunable reward channels within a fixed acceptance contract. Consultants annotate methods, branches, bounded loops, checkpoints, relative comparisons, and report refinement; a registry records applicable evidence. Adaptation revises configurations or trains a separate controller or skill while freezing the foundation executor. Independent hard gates govern qualification; RL and preference methods optimize candidates without supplying factual truth. Qualification and held-out improvement over the unchanged target are separate outcomes. Supplied intent labels permit a limited paired recount: small prompt/retry gains coexist with regressions and failed gates. FinQA supplements match prior summaries and retain provena

fc202d880270a5c6394addcc.title_original: CompMat-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Computational Materials Science
fc202d880270a5c6394addcc.excerpt: arXiv:2610.00636v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evaluating AI agents on scientific research tasks is constrained by the time and resources required for the underlying experiments or calculations. In computational materials research, repeating the same expensive simulations across agents and trials can make evaluation impractical. We introduce CompMat-Bench, a benchmark of 94 tasks derived from recently published computational materials studies, each asking agents to complete a step toward achieving the study's scientific goal. We reproduce the research steps in advance and assess agents on preparing inputs and analyzing outputs for expensive simulations, so expensive simulations can be avoided during evaluation. The reproduced inputs and results serve as ground truth for grading agents with fixed rules, without an LLM judge. The benchmark supports four evaluation conditions: single tasks and workflows composed of related tasks, each with full or reduced methodological guidance. With full guidance on single tasks, agents based on three LLMs demonstrate the ability to complete individual materials research steps, with pass rates of 66.0-90.4% across 94 tasks. Both longer workflows and reduced guidance can limit agent performance, but in different ways for different agents: they lower the pass rates of the weaker agents, whereas the strongest agent falls only when a long workflow is combined with reduced guidance. Failure analysis attributes most failures to scientific error

8bb6c65a87bca6e143201351.title_original: Global Coherence: When Every Agent Is Right and the Team Is Still Wrong - A Local-to-Global Semantic Foundation for Multi-Agent Collaboration
8bb6c65a87bca6e143201351.excerpt: arXiv:2610.02036v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI agents can each make locally valid decisions yet jointly produce an invalid result. We call this the global coherence problem: a failure of shared state, not merely of intelligence. Our Observation-Aliasing Impossibility Theorem gives the exact boundary. A policy can guarantee a valid action exactly when all worlds producing the same observation share an admissible action. If k indistinguishable worlds require pairwise-disjoint actions, the best randomized worst-case success is 1/k; more reasoning, roles, messages, or samples cannot recover the missing distinction. A stronger model can reason better within its context, but it cannot see beyond it. The smallest sufficient context is NP-hard to find, yet counterexample-guided refinement finds a sufficient one and recertifies it as rules change. We give local-to-global runtime semantics X = (H, C, G, F; D): topology H records overlapping scopes; category C governs state-changing actions; groupoid G keeps reversible translations; sheaf F tests whether local views glue into one world; and history D keeps only what alters legal futures. Each preserves the needed information as state is split, translated, or changed. Models propose; the harness owns shared state and governs commit. Ten studies test the boundary. On a revision benchmark, a frontier model scores 40/40 when the deciding event is visible; hidden, every arm is consistent with chance (1/3); one restored fact returns 4

9400f120b27b6331866b9de0.excerpt: arXiv:2610.03198v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The memory footprint of the key-value (KV) cache constrains the practical use of long-context models, and it dominates cost when one prefilled context must later serve many different queries. In this reusable setting, query-agnostic compression trades cost against quality: lightweight estimators are cheap but less accurate, whereas full-context reconstruction scoring is more accurate yet reprocesses the entire prompt. We introduce KV$^2$, a query-agnostic KV-cache compression method based on selective reconstruction. KV$^2$ first uses a lightweight proxy scorer to identify informative in-context tokens, then reprocesses only this subset to compute final eviction scores. On RULER, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and LongBench, KV$^2$'s margin over baselines widens as the budget tightens: on RULER 16K at a 2% KV-cache budget it improves the average score over the next-best baseline by more than 40 percentage points, and on LongBench it attains the highest average across 2%-10% budgets at lower compression-stage runtime and peak memory than full-context reconstruction. Reusable KV-cache compression thus does not require reprocessing the full context. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/KVsquared-0B97.

2ca4b354aaf1746d0eaf904f.title_original: Video-Time Priors for EEG-fNIRS Emotion Regression on Familiar Videos
2ca4b354aaf1746d0eaf904f.excerpt: arXiv:2610.03618v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Do viewer-specific physiological signals improve continuous emotion regression beyond the stimulus-driven response shared across viewers? We examine this question by predicting emotion ratings for new viewers watching videos that also appear in the training set. As a stimulus-only baseline, we define a video-time prior:the smoothed median of training labels for each video at each second. We then combine this prior, using a fixed fusion weight, with a graph-based model of electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) signals. On MER-PS 2026, five-fold cross-validation grouped by participant over 24 participants yields a mean absolute error (MAE) of 29.01 for fusion, compared with 29.06 for the prior alone. On an external cohort of four participants excluded from training, the corresponding MAEs are 27.72 and 28.04. In this cohort, most of the MAE reduction relative to a global-constant baseline comes from the prior, that is, from video identity and playback time alone.Fusion lowers MAE for three of the four held-out participants and for nine of the fifteen videos. The added value of physiological signals is therefore small and varies across participants and videos. Because the model uses physiological signals recorded after each prediction time, it supports only offline prediction. Generalization to unseen videos remains untested.

f26320a53ed4d8cebd7f6d2b.title_original: Asynchrony Is Nearly Free for Evolution Strategies on Long-Horizon LLM Agentic Tasks
f26320a53ed4d8cebd7f6d2b.excerpt: arXiv:2610.04196v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Synchronous policy updates can limit the efficiency of post-training for long-horizon LLM agents. When trajectories span multiple interaction turns, completion times can vary substantially, and synchronous update barriers leave faster workers idling, wasting compute resources. Asynchronous reinforcement learning addresses this inefficiency but introduces policy lag and off-policy optimization. Evolution strategies (ES) are a backpropagation-free alternative to gradient-based training, yet require many perturbed-policy evaluations and have remained largely synchronous in current LLM post-training. We introduce bounded-staleness asynchronous ES and investigate its training behavior under stale fitness measurements. On WebShop, we systematically vary the lag and fraction of stale fitness measurements and additionally introduce two stress tests to probe extreme staleness cases. Natural asynchrony closely tracks synchronous ES, and degradation in evaluation accuracy remains small even under extreme staleness, including when all fitness measurements are stale. These findings suggest that ES can tolerate substantial policy staleness without explicit off-policy correction, supporting its use in asynchronous post-training for long-horizon LLM agents.

b586f2a173336380eb27845d.title_original: SCOPE: Certified Theorem Proving with a Language Model as the Policy Planner
b586f2a173336380eb27845d.excerpt: arXiv:2610.08319v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In proof assistants such as Lean, a generated proof must pass machine compilation checks, so evaluation needs no human scoring. Direct generation fails on multi-step numeric propositions: a proof is valid only if every content integer is correct, so the pass rate is bounded by the k-th power of the per-integer accuracy. Controlled corruption across 2,617 reference proofs confirms this power law. SCOPE (State-Conditioned Operator Planning and Execution) enforces the natural division of labor: the model plans over an operator vocabulary, a symbolic engine executes the numerics, and a compiler renders the proof. On a 218-problem suite it certifies 191/218 (87.6%) with a 135M backbone; the 7B DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5-RL certifies 18/218 at 27.5 times the tokens and 37.5 times the wall-clock, and DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B certifies zero on a bidirectional dual suite. Multi-step thinking costs 6.12 discrete decision actions per problem and produces no natural-language thinking text. Replacing the lagged engine state in the decision frame with the current one lifts the pass rate from 117/218 to 191/218, while up-weighting the chain-end loss hurts. On the public Lean-Workbook library, 2,132 of 3,536 gradeable admissible problems certify (60.29%) with zero regression on the main suite. All readings come from a version-frozen review with independent rechecks and reverse verification. Restricting free generation and keeping decision-time infor

6913f2260c2f63322da7795d.title_original: ParanoiaEval: Benchmarking Unnecessary Defensive Work in Agentic Coding
6913f2260c2f63322da7795d.excerpt: arXiv:2610.08662v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As coding agents increasingly undertake real-world work autonomously, judging whether their risk treatments are warranted has become important. Existing work evaluates related agent behaviors from separate perspectives, but lacks a systematic framework for unifying these behaviors. To bridge this gap, we introduce ParanoiaEval, the first benchmark for unified evaluation of risk-treatment capabilities in coding agents. Grounded in the well-established Avoidance-Transfer-Mitigation-Acceptance framework in software engineering risk management, ParanoiaEval operationalizes its 4 fundamental treatments for coding-agent settings and contains 200 evidence-controlled repository-level task pairs, each differing only in treatment-defining evidence. We further introduce dedicated metrics for risk-treatment violations and evidence responsiveness, using a human-calibrated agentic judge for reliable evaluation. Large-scale experiments on 8 representative models and a post-hoc human study reveal that (I) unnecessary risk treatment occurs in 11.2%-58.7% of runs despite explicit evidence, with substantial variation across agent configurations; (II) stronger task capability does not ensure more appropriate risk treatment, while treatment violations substantially harm developers' experience, establishing risk treatment as an independent capability dimension; and (III) agents exhibit systematic patterns consistent with established risk-manageme

3d57d1660c1c76d9766065fd.title_original: Distributionally Robust Regularization of Sparse Integer Programming Trained Learning Models
3d57d1660c1c76d9766065fd.excerpt: arXiv:2311.01994v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Building explainable machine learning models is crucial for human users to be able to interpret the proposed statistical relationship obtained from the training data. Mixed-integer optimization formulations are often used to train such models with explicit sparsity constraints, aiming to strike the right trade-off between sparsity and prediction accuracy. Existing methods to find the right choice of sparsity -- e.g., via cross-validation -- are computationally expensive. For convex model training formulations, recent advances in distributionally robust optimization (DRO) provide strong generalization while sidestepping this computational burden. We describe an extension of such regularization via DRO to mixed-integer sparse programs, providing statistical guarantees as a function of an associated sparsity parameter of the formulation. We illustrate the use of this approach in the case of building explainable binary classification models using sets of feature value rules.

0909d56c4df04cd4b11a06b9.title_original: InkSight: Offline-to-Online Handwriting Conversion by Teaching Vision-Language Models to Read and Write
0909d56c4df04cd4b11a06b9.excerpt: arXiv:2402.05804v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Digital note-taking is gaining popularity, offering a durable, editable, and easily indexable way of storing notes in a vectorized form, known as digital ink. However, a substantial gap remains between this way of note-taking and traditional pen-and-paper note-taking, a practice that is still favored by a vast majority. Our work InkSight, aims to bridge the gap by empowering physical note-takers to effortlessly convert their work (offline handwriting) to digital ink (online handwriting), a process we refer to as derendering. Prior research on the topic has focused on the geometric properties of images, resulting in limited generalization beyond their training domains. Our approach combines reading and writing priors, allowing training a model in the absence of large amounts of paired samples, which are difficult to obtain. To our knowledge, this is the first work that effectively derenders handwritten text in arbitrary photos with diverse visual characteristics and backgrounds. Furthermore, it generalizes beyond its training domain into simple sketches. Our human evaluation reveals that 87% of the samples produced by our model on the challenging HierText dataset are considered as a valid tracing of the input image and 67% look like a pen trajectory traced by a human.

75a51ce64cda3c75d96c065c.excerpt: arXiv:2406.20031v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Pairwise difference learning (PDL) has recently been introduced as a new meta-learning technique for regression. Instead of learning a mapping from instances to outcomes in the standard way, the key idea is to learn a function that takes two instances as input and predicts the difference between the respective outcomes. Given a function of this kind, predictions for a query instance are derived from every training example and then averaged. This paper extends PDL toward the task of classification and proposes a meta-learning technique for inducing a PDL classifier by solving a suitably defined (binary) classification problem on a paired version of the original training data. We analyze the performance of the PDL classifier in a large-scale empirical study and find that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of prediction performance. Last but not least, we provide an easy-to-use and publicly available implementation of PDL in a Python package.

358f8b21b8c643fb845e2c87.title_original: LLMR: Knowledge Distillation with a Large Language Model-Induced Reward
358f8b21b8c643fb845e2c87.excerpt: arXiv:2409.12500v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models have become increasingly popular and demonstrated remarkable performance in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, these models are typically computationally expensive and difficult to be deployed in resource-constrained environments. In this paper, we propose LLMR, a novel knowledge distillation (KD) method based on a reward function induced from large language models. We conducted experiments on multiple datasets in the dialogue generation and summarization tasks. Empirical results demonstrate that our LLMR approach consistently outperforms traditional KD methods in different tasks and datasets.

c5f43538560791d69ea6776e.title_original: STAMP: Symmetric Temporal Averaging Message Passing for Domain Adaptation in Chronologically Split Graphs
c5f43538560791d69ea6776e.excerpt: arXiv:2411.10957v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper addresses domain adaptation in graph-structured data under chronological splits. We consider transductive semi-supervised node classification (SSNC), in which labels of historical nodes are used to predict labels of more recent nodes. Temporal dependencies in graph connectivity induce distribution shifts across time, often degrading the performance of models trained on past nodes. Despite its practical relevance, domain adaptation under chronological graph splits remains relatively underexplored. We propose Symmetric Temporal Averaging Message Passing (STAMP), a timestamp-balanced operator that replaces standard neighborhood aggregation with temporally aligned propagation. We call its specialized variant for the heterogeneous ogbn-mag dataset STAMP-mag, reserving STAMP for the general formulation. By balancing messages across timestamps, STAMP enforces first-moment invariance across temporal domains while remaining scalable and easy to implement. Unlike many existing domain adaptation methods, whose assumptions are difficult to verify on graphs, STAMP relies on transparent, practically checkable conditions and is supported by theoretical analysis. Empirically, STAMP and STAMP-mag improve accuracy across all evaluated temporal graph benchmarks. STAMP achieves state-of-the-art performance on ogbn-arxiv, while STAMP-mag does so on ogbn-mag. For temporal-split Pokec, where no established benchmark exists, applyi

dc305f72e97753ad2f1c2eca.title_original: A self-learning framework for adaptive free-form pipe routing in aeroengines
dc305f72e97753ad2f1c2eca.excerpt: arXiv:2504.03669v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Pipe routing is a highly complex, time-consuming, and no-deterministic polynomial-time hard (NP-hard) problem in aeroengine design. Despite extensive research efforts in optimizing constant-curvature pipe routing, the growing demand for free-form pipes poses new challenges. Dynamic design environments and fuzzy layout rules further impact the optimization performance and efficiency. To tackle these challenges, this study proposes a self-learning-based method (SLPR) for optimizing free-form pipe routing in aeroengines. The SLPR is based on the proximal policy optimization (PPO) algorithm and integrates a unified rule modeling framework for efficient obstacle detection and fuzzy rule modeling in continuous space. Additionally, a potential energy table is constructed to enable rapid queries of layout tendencies and interference. The agent within SLPR iteratively refines pipe routing and accumulates the design knowledge through interaction with the environment. Once the design environment shifts, the agent can swiftly adapt by fine-tuning network parameters. Comparative tests reveal that SLPR ensures smooth pipe routing through cubic non-uniform B-spline (NURBS) curves, avoiding redundant pipe segments found in constant-curvature pipe routing. Results in both static and dynamic design environments demonstrate that SLPR outperforms three representative baselines in terms of the pipe length reduction, the adherence to layout

8e5dee7b5eb1600b7c2bbc6f.title_original: Towards Reliable Long-Context Reasoning: Detecting Unanswerable Questions via FactGuard
8e5dee7b5eb1600b7c2bbc6f.excerpt: arXiv:2504.05607v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Despite the success of Large Language Models (LLMs) in long-context tasks, their reliability in recognizing unanswerable questions remains a critical challenge. In information-seeking scenarios, models often suffer from overconfidence and hallucinations when evidence is missing or misleading. In this paper, we propose FACTGUARD, a systematic multi-task workflow for generating evidence-grounded answerable and unanswerable questions. We introduce FACTGUARD-BENCH, a benchmark comprising 25,220 examples with context lengths up to 128K, specifically targeting Lack of Evidence and Misleading Evidence scenarios. Evaluations of eleven representative open-source and proprietary LLMs reveal a significant reliability gap: models struggle to reject unanswerable questions as context scales, with the leading model achieving only 71.62% accuracy. By training with FACTGUARD-BENCH, we improve overall accuracy to 81.17% and significantly enhance models' reasoned rejection capabilities. Our work provides a scalable path toward building more faithful and trustworthy long-context LLMs. Our source is publicly available at https://github.com/biaoliu-kiritsugu/FactGuard.

93c4e1186ada4b0e83f6763a.title_original: PanoDiff-SR: Synthesizing Dental Panoramic Radiographs using Diffusion and Super-resolution
93c4e1186ada4b0e83f6763a.excerpt: arXiv:2507.09227v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Interest in generating realistic synthetic medical images has grown in recent years. Such datasets can mitigate the scarcity of public data for artificial intelligence research and support education. Work on synthesizing dental panoramic radiographs (PRs) has so far relied almost exclusively on generative adversarial networks (GANs), and three limitations recur: the synthesized field of view is often restricted to a cropped dentoalveolar region rather than a complete PR; observer studies of GAN-generated PRs report that clinicians still identify synthetic images with accuracies of roughly 78-82%, implying persistent visible giveaways; and adversarial training remains sensitive to instability and mode collapse. Generating a full-size PR directly at diagnostic resolution with a diffusion model is an alternative, but sampling at that resolution is costly. We therefore present PanoDiff-SR, an end-to-end two-stage pipeline developed and evaluated specifically for panoramic radiography: a denoising diffusion implicit model (PanoDiff) generates a low-resolution (LR) seed PR ($256\times128$), which a fine-tuned hybrid attention transformer (HAT) super-resolution (SR) stage upscales to a high-resolution (HR) PR of $1024\times512$. Decoupling the expensive generative step from the resolution step yields complete, full-arch PRs at diagnostic resolution on a single 47 GB GPU.
